messages.subject: Problems with SPDE model
messages.subject_clean: Problems with SPDE model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I already posted into this group last week <http://www.r-inla.org/comments-1?place=topic%2Fr-inla-discussion-group%2FCRZOdA_OOEI%2Fdiscussion> to ask for help with a dynamic spatio-temporal AR model. I currently fit an SPDE model following the instructions that I found in several documents and the paper by Cameletti et al (2012). However INLA always crahses when I enlarge my dataset beyond a (to me) unknown threshold and Windows gives the error: "inla.exe has stopped working". After I select "close program" I get the additional warning message from the verbose output:

running command '"\\icnas1.cc.ic.ac.uk/sft16/R/win-library/3.3/INLA/bin/windows/64bit/inla.exe <http://icnas1.cc.ic.ac.uk/sft16/R/win-library/3.3/INLA/bin/windows/64bit/inla.exe>"  -b -s -v  "C:/Users/SFT16/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpQB7vaS/fileb857be763/Model.ini"' had status 253

I attached the full verbose output of a working model (currently 10 stations, mesh with 25 knots and 478 days) and two verbose outputs of models that do not work (also 10 stations, mesh with 25 knots and 479 days). Do you have any idea why INLA crashes?

Furthermore, I am slightly confused about the results of the model that works. It is a hierarchical model of the form:

Z(s,t)= Y(s,t) + e(s,t); e(s,t) ~ iid Gaussian
Y(s,t)= rho * Y(s,t-1) + eps(s,t); eps(s,t) ~ temporal independent, spatially coloured Gaussian

The empirical autocorrelation in the observed stationwise data z usually lies around 0.7. However, the posterior of the AR coefficient rho is estimated by the model to be very close to 1. Can such a posterior be the result of a wrong SPDE approximation of the GF and is this an unusual estimate?

Thank you for your help!
Stephan

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Many of us were at the same conference last week, so didn't have a chance to look at this fully.

You should probably check if using  inla.spde2.pcmatern instead inla.spde2.matern works better for the small model, as it looks like your parameter estimates walk away in a weird direction. The pcmatern model has a better prior distribution for the parameters.  Can you please state formula code for the model as well, as I suspect there might be some issue there as well. (Also include any inla.stack code etc, and the inla() call itself)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

thank you - I will try out the inla.spde2.pcmatern function tomorrow. My code for the model construction is the following:

# Contruct mesh:
ana.mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(loc = coordinates(MS.loc[c(new.control.stations, predict.station)]),
                       loc.domain = coordinates(LDN.union@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]),
                       max.edge = c(50*1000))

# Mesh to spde
matern.alpha<-1.5
ana.spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = ana.mesh, alpha = matern.alpha)

# A
ana.A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=ana.mesh,
                          loc=coordinates(MS.loc[data.ana$code]),
                          group=data.ana$time2,
                          n.group = max(data.ana$time2))

# Produce indices
ana.indices<-inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde=ana.spde$n.spde, n.group = max(data.ana$time2))

# Prepare data stack for inla:
ana.stack <- inla.stack(tag='ana',
                        data=list(logNOX=data.ana$nox.na <http://nox.na>),
                        A=list(ana.A,1),
                        effects=list(c(list(intercept = rep(1, ana.mesh$n)),ana.indices),
                                     list(ws=data.ana$ws,
                                          solar = data.ana$solar,
                                          rain = data.ana$rain,
                                          temp=data.ana$temp,
                                          bp = data.ana$bp,
                                          rhum = data.ana$rhum,
                                          code = data.ana$code,
                                          trend = data.ana$trend,
                                          i = data.ana$ID)))

inla.data.ana<-inla.stack.data(ana.stack, SPDE = ana.spde)

# Generate summary list
model.simp<-list()

#Simple Model without covariates (except station specific intercept):
model.simp$formula <- logNOX ~ 0 + code + f(field, model= SPDE, group=field.group, control.group=list(model="ar1")) + f(i, model = "iid")

model.simp$inla <- inla(model.simp$formula,
                        data = inla.data.ana ,
                        family = "gaussian",
                        control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy='inla'),
                        control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(ana.stack), compute = T),
                        control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(param=c(1,20), fixed = T))),
                        debug = F,
                        verbose = T)

messages.body_plain:
I think it should be. "code" is a station specific factor which allows for a station specific intercept (in the smaller model, which works, these coefficients are estimated in a sensible manner).
"i/ID" varies for each observation and the corresponding iid effect is intended to mimic the random noise eps(s,t) since the noise in the control.family argument is fixed to a relatively small value. (Somewhere in the INLA group I read that this is a way to do predictions that include observational noise) However inla also crashes when I remove the iid effect on "i/ID" and allow the noise to be estimated.

messages.body_plain:
I think the problem with estimating the zero probability in the zeroinflatedpoisson0 is that you are already inferring zero-probabilities in the bernoulli likelihood. So this parameter may not be identifiable.

Can you try zeroinflatedpoisson0, but fixing the zero probability parameter, e.g. to the empirical estimate? (Take care of the internal parametrisation).

Kind regards,
Haakon

On 30 July 2017 at 19:52, Rujia Bi <crysta...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Agree.
>
> Sent from my iPhone

>

>

> >
> >
> > On Sunday, July 30, 2017 at 12:53:25 PM UTC+1, Haakon Bakka wrote:
> > > I am not sure if your use of zeroinflatedpoisson0 is correct.
> > >
> > > Usually for Hurdle models: Where there are 0's the "poisson-part" has an NA observation. The reasoning is that you do not know what it would have been if it had made the "hurdle" of crossing zero.
> >
> > Hello...
> >
> > It would either be:
> >
> > family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0"
> >
> > for a Poisson hurdle model (which means that the binary part is modelled as a function of an intercept...with no covariates..and the count part as a function of covariates).....or
> >
> > family=c(’binomial’, ’zerotruncatedPoisson’)
> >
> > where the first column of the response variable consists of 0 and 1, and the second column of the response variable contains only the non-zero data  (and the rest is set to NA). The problem is that INLA does not have a zero truncated Poisson distribution....so
> > zerotruncatedPoisson will not work. Hence......I am not sure how you can put covariates in the binary part of the model.
> >
> > There are examples in the INLA literature in which this is done for continuous data (rainfall)....but in that example a gamma distribution is used for the non-zero data...and the gamma distribution is already zero truncated. So..there is works.
> >
> > It would be nice if the zero truncated Poisson/NB distributions could be added to INLA....or if someone can tell me that I am wrong.
> >
> > Kind regards,
> >
> > Alain Zuur
> > www.highstat.com <http://www.highstat.com>
> >
> >

> > >
> > > So I believe you should exchange your zeroinflatedpoisson for a poisson, or a poisson where the zeroes are removed.
> > >
> > > PS. You could end up with similar results through different approaches, but estimating the zero-probability will get you in trouble if you have "NA and positive data".
> > >
> > > Kind regards,
> > > Haakon Bakka
> > >

> > > >
> > > > Thanks,
> > > > Ruby

You can't. All zero inflated distributions in INLA assume a single zero inflation parameter (an intercept only model for the zero inflation part).

ir. Thierry Onkelinx

team Biometrie & Kwaliteitszorg / team Biometrics & Quality Assurance

1070 Anderlecht
Belgium

On 02/08/2017 10:28, Rujia Bi wrote:
> Sorry, I can't understand... If use zeroinflatedpoisson0, how can I add covariates on the binary part?
>

You can model both parts with covariates + random effects + parmetric non-linear effects in INLA having or not shared components (if not, model separated). Haakon give you insight on this. Basically, you can build one linear predictor for the zeros and another for the positives. You may follow an example for the zero-gamma case in the INLA book.
Elias

messages.body_plain:
On 02/08/2017 14:36, Rujia Bi wrote:
> It is the reason why I did not use zeroinflatedpoisson0...

You can try and ask the INLA team very friendly whether they can add the zero truncated Poisson distribution to R-INLA. Its likelihood function is nearly the same as that of the Poisson....except for a 1 / (1 - exp(-mu_i)) term. Assuming that the (spatial) random effects in the Bernoulli part and the (spatial) random effects in the zero truncated Poisson part are independent of each other, then you/R-INLA can estimate the parameters of the two components separately....and once you have the two parts of the hurdle model, you can easily work out the mean and the variance of the actual hurdle model.

Alain

> > > > > > > I am not sure if your use of zeroinflatedpoisson0 is correct.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Usually for Hurdle models: Where there are 0's the "poisson-part" has an NA observation. The reasoning is that you do not know what it would have been if it had made the "hurdle" of crossing zero.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hello...
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It would either be:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0"
> > > > > >
> > > > > > for a Poisson hurdle model (which means that the binary part is modelled as a function of an intercept...with no covariates..and the count part as a function of covariates).....or
> > > > > >
> > > > > > family=c(’binomial’, ’zerotruncatedPoisson’)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > where the first column of the response variable consists of 0 and 1, and the second column of the response variable contains only the non-zero data  (and the rest is set to NA). The problem is that INLA does not have a zero truncated Poisson distribution....so
> > > > > > zerotruncatedPoisson will not work. Hence......I am not sure how you can put covariates in the binary part of the model.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > There are examples in the INLA literature in which this is done for continuous data (rainfall)....but in that example a gamma distribution is used for the non-zero data...and the gamma distribution is already zero truncated. So..there is works.

> > > > > > It would be nice if the zero truncated Poisson/NB distributions could be added to INLA....or if someone can tell me that I am wrong.

> > > > > > Kind regards,

messages.body_plain:
I played a bit with your example. I've used dplyr for the data wrangling which makes it IMHO more readable.

More importantly I wanted to investigate the effect of the prior of the zero inflated part. It turns out that it has fixing it at 10 or -10 yields the same parameter estimates for the count process, the same fitted values and the same WAIC. I am not sure if that is what we would expect...
Using the default prior yields a \theta estimate of -5.8 (-8.2, -4.1). The parameter estimates for the count process are equivalent (differences <1e-7 for the mean, <1e-5 for the quantiles). Differences in mean fitted values were < 1e-4. The waic was, to my surprise, much lower.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm wondering how to code a non-nested model in which some data points are part of multiple groups to be modeled as random effects.

Here is an example of the table:

        s         age  s12 s13 s14 s23 s24 s34
    1: 1   3.390124   1   0   0   0   0   0
    2: 1   7.380292   1   0   0   0   0   0
    3: 0 19.696835   1   0   0   1   1   0
    4: 1 26.935525   1   0   0   0   0   0
    5: 0   6.533801   1   0   0   1   1   0
 ---
890: 1   4.918274   0   0   0   0   0   1
891: 1   3.431649   0   0   0   0   0   1
892: 0 17.627162   0   1   0   1   0   1
893: 1   6.403289   0   0   0   0   0   1
894: 0   5.766497   0   0   1   0   1   1

I want to model a logistic regression in which ```s ~ age```, but want to add the group structure observed in the columns sXX. You can see that some data points are only from one sXX (e.g., the first row is member of s13), while others correspond to more than 1 sXX (e.g., row three is member of s13, s23 and s24).

In a non-multi-membership model, I would just code columns sXX to and id from 1 to 6.

How is the way to code, if possible, such a multi-membership model?

I would much appreciate any help in this regard.

On 08/05/2017 01:31 PM, Paul Lantos wrote:
> It's now doing this unpredictably with other binary variables. I'm now getting this without having changed the model at all other than trying it without the "gender variable"
> nicu0  -1.4892 18.2637   -37.3471  -1.4898    34.3387 -1.4892   0
> nicu1  -1.1172 18.2644   -36.9763  -1.1177    34.7120 -1.1172   0

Here you have a singular model. It is all about the contrast parametrization, not an INLA issue. Consider the following example:

 n = 10;
 dat = data.frame(ga=runif(n),
  race=factor(rbinom(n,1,.5)),
  gender=as.factor(rbinom(n,1,0.5)),
  b0=rep(1,n))
model.matrix(~ga+gender+race, dat)[1:2,]
model.matrix(~0+b0+ga+gender+race, dat)[1:2,]

In the second case, b0=gender0+gender1, so a linear combination leading to a singularity.

Elias

When running with inla.stack, you also use expand.factor.strategy="inla", right?
Also see Elias post, which showed what happens when the intercept is a regular covariates (as it must be for inla.stack to operate properly).

Håvard, I think we need an expand.factor.strategy="inla0", meaning "drop the first level of every factor" (I think the current "inla" strategy does something different to that, that only works sensibly when there is a single factor in the model...).

Paul, you can have full control over the factor level handling if you convert the factors yourself into model matrices instead when supplying them to inla.stack. (Only works for factors not involved in an f() model)
Something like
  ..., effects=list(list(myfactor=model.matrix(~0+thefactor, data)[,-1],  ...)), ..

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The issue with factors and inla.stack is the handling of NAs. Even if there are no NAs in the input data, inla.stack necessarily by construction introduces NAs, and that can lead to issues later on inside inla(). From what I remember, inla() will abort or warn in at least some situations, telling the user to use expand.factor.strategy="inla". But as I explained in an earlier email, that doesn't quite do what you want when you have more than one factor.

So a safer method is to convert the factors yourself, as then you have complete control (even though the prior distribution is then not symmetric in the original levels). Or to use f(myfactor, model="iid", constr=TRUE), which keeps the symmetry, and makes the model non-singular by imposing a sum-to-zero constraint on the coefficients.

Finn

                      data=list(y=data$Random),

                                        bw=data$bw_std,
                                        nicu=data$nicu,
                                        parity=data$parity_std,
                                        sti=data$sti)))

stk.pred <- inla.stack(tag='prediction',
                       data=list(y=NA),
                       A=list(A.pred, 1),
                       effects=list(s=1:spde2$n.spde,
                                    list(b0=1,

                                         gender=grid$gender,
                                         bw=grid$bw_std,
                                         nicu=grid$nicu,
                                         parity=grid$parity_std,
                                         sti=grid$sti)))

stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)

  f(s, model=spde2)+

  f(sti, model="iid", constr=TRUE)+
  f(race, model="iid", constr=TRUE)+

messages.body_plain:
The key is that it is the _first_ of the factor variables;
Identifiability is an agelong issue with factor models in general, since if each level for each factor has its own, independent and unconstrained, coefficient, any model with two factors would be nonidentifiable. In addition, any model with an intercept and a factor would also be nonidentifiable.

Several solutions to this are used in practice.

One is to impose constraints (see my earlier email for how to use that approach in inla).

Another is to remove enough  coefficients to make the model identifiable, typically by removing the first level of all the factor covariates, in the case of a model with an intercept, or all but the first factor, in the case of a model with no intercept.
Since inla relies on a basic R model.matrix() that has no way of detecting that b0 is really an intercept, the first level of the first factor is kept in your model, even though it should more reasonably have been removed.
Removing b0 from the model should make it identifiable.

Finn

Guess I can't do it with all 0 (it requires more than one level), but I did rbinom(n, 1, 0.5) to generate random 1s and 0s, which for a sample with 19,384 observations should really not affect the model. I put it first in the data stack and in the formula. Will see how that works.

> > Identifiability is an agelong issue with factor models in general, since if each level for each factor has its own, independent and unconstrained, coefficient, any model with two factors would be nonidentifiable. In addition, any model with an intercept and a factor would also be nonidentifiable.
> >
> > Several solutions to this are used in practice.
> >
> > One is to impose constraints (see my earlier email for how to use that approach in inla).
> >
> > Another is to remove enough  coefficients to make the model identifiable, typically by removing the first level of all the factor covariates, in the case of a model with an intercept, or all but the first factor, in the case of a model with no intercept.
> > Since inla relies on a basic R model.matrix() that has no way of detecting that b0 is really an intercept, the first level of the first factor is kept in your model, even though it should more reasonably have been removed.
> > Removing b0 from the model should make it identifiable.

Minor differences in the DIC is to be expected, simply because of the
parallel computing. If the posterior is very flat, then the impact can
be larger.  if you expect a flat posterior, you can try to do

r = inla(...)
r = inla.rerun(r)

which will restart at the current mode, which usually would stabalize
the results.

If there are any differences beyond this, please let me know.

On 10 Aug 2017, at 06:03, Rujia Bi <crysta...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Intercept, some fixed effects, random year effect (RW2)

The parameters often need to be considered together; e.g., the spde variance parameter and the observation variance need to be considered, as they necessarily interact differently in different models.

The number of observations doesn't impact the field variance as such. The number of observations would rather have an effect on the uncertainties.
But on possible interpretation is that the the non-replicated model you are essentially modeling the temporally averaged version of the fields in the replication model, which should be expected to have a smaller variance. But this then interacts with the observation variance, as well as the correlation range parameter, so it's not trivial to interpret.

I have two suggestions:

1. use the scaled version of the intrinsic 'rw2' effect (see
http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211675313000407) and
a penalized complexity prior for its precision (see
http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ss/1491465621)

2. instead of having 'besag' replicated + 'iid' not replicated, you can
have a bit more flexible one replicating a 'bym' model. However, use
'bym2' because it has a nicer interpretation, as you can see in
http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/0962280216660421

### code suggestion
pcprec <- list(prec=list(prior="pcprec", params=c(1, 0.01)))
ff <- count ~ f(inla.group(crppland), model="rw2",
                 scale.model=TRUE, hyper=pcprec, replicate=yr.id2) +
     f(key, model="bym2", graph="bbsquail2.graph", replicate=yr.id <http://yr.id>)
rr <- inla(ff, family="poisson", data=inp3yr,
            control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE))

Elias

Not completely sure what this is about, but
- The DIC is not a good measure for spatial models (p \approx n)
- Personally, I prefer to set the median (instead of the 0.01 quantile)
- Testing for no-effect is very difficult, as how you design the test depends on what you mean

## Testing for no effect
What should happen if the data is indifferent to the use of a model component? (I.e. sigma is not identifiable from the data) Should the test give "model component not needed" (sigma=0), or "model component not rejected" (sigma != 0) ?

I would go with prior-posterior plots of sigma, unless you have specific requirements.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
The problem looks like numerical instability (I'm sure Håvard can
explain more). The solution is to scale your variables (and also make
sure the number of successes is an integer!). This also shortens your
credible intervals, which makes all the gods of marginalisation happy:

library(INLA)
library(data.table)

# read in toy data
allData <- fread("toyData.csv")
allData$N <- allData$sp1*allData$nTrials
allData$bioclim1.sc <http://bioclim1.sc> <- scale(allData$bioclim1)

# subset data for points where we have observations
obsData <- allData[!is.na <http://is.na>(sp1), ]

# define formula
formula <- N ~ bioclim1.sc <http://bioclim1.sc> + I(bioclim1.sc <http://bioclim1.sc>^2)

testModel_1 <- inla(formula,
    data = obsData,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = obsData$nTrials,
    control.predictor = list(compute = T),
    control.compute = list(dic = T))

testModel_2 <- inla(formula,
    data = allData,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = allData$nTrials,
    control.predictor = list(compute = T),
    control.compute = list(dic = T))

summary(testModel_1)
summary(testModel_2)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] PC prior for Matern models
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] PC prior for Matern models
messages.body_plain:
I think you will see a random plot like that anyway, since the "s" is arbitrarily located in space...?

For a time series (or nonlinear covariate) you should see some structure, but space is 2-dimensionsal.

The point I was making was about the design of the "test", since you have to decide what outcome you want in cases with a flat likelihood. The usual is to say "cannot reject null hypothesis", but this depends on whether null is "effect" or "no effect". If null is "no effect", then you will conclude "no effect" from a flat likelihood, which may or may not be reasonable.

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.subject_clean: Credibility intervals for linear predictor conditional on random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Is there a way to simulate predictions with inla that are conditional on the mean random effect in a random effects model?
For instance, I have a model like this:
inla(y ~ x +
            f(grp, model = "iid"),
    data = dmod, family = "gaussian",
    control.predictor = list(link = 1))

Where x is a continuous covaraite and grp is a factor giving group levels. I want to get the 95% CIs for values of y across the range of x values, conditional on the mean value of 'grp' (ie = 0).
e.g. if using frequentist inference, you can do this with the lme4 package by boostrapping over the covariate but not the random effects (ie bootMer this is the option use.u = TRUE).

A reproducible example is given here:  https://github.com/cbrown5/uncertainty-intervals/blob/master/inla-marginal-conditional-intervals.R
Also see figures here: https://github.com/cbrown5/uncertainty-intervals

I know INLA derives its convenience by estimating only the marginals, but I had though that inla.posterior.sample() might be the solution, however it seems the quantiles of the posterior samples are also marginals.

Thanks,
Chris

messages.body_plain:
I am running a binomial model and I get a huge sd on the intercept when a spatial random field is introduced in the model. The response is a species presence absence variable and for this example I only utilize continuous covariates. I am struggling for quite some time with this and I cannot figure out whether this is a dataset related problem or not. For the moment I am using a coarse mesh, but I intend to utilize a finer mesh with land barriers as these are fisheries data, as well as to include factors in the model (already read and used Elias' instructions in this post ''Factor vs Numeric / Integer for binomial model'' in the list).

#load(test.RData)
library(INLA);
INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()
inla.setOption(num.threads = 30)
dataset_name = 'testdata.csv'
X <- read.csv(file = paste0(workdir, 'INLA/INLAinput/', dataset_name))
X$fYEAR <- as.factor(X$fYEAR)
X$fSPF <- as.factor(X$fSPF)
trainLoc <- cbind(X$Xkm.std, X$Ykm.std)
ConvHull <- inla.nonconvex.hull(trainLoc, convex = 200, resolution=c(75,75))
mesh.a <- inla.mesh.2d(max.edge = c(200,400), cutoff = 100, boundary = ConvHull)
#plot(mesh.a, lwd=1, asp=1, main='')
#points(trainLoc, col = X$MAC_PrAb+1, pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

############################################
spde.a <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh.a, alpha = 2)
A.1 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh.a, loc = trainLoc)
ind.1 <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 's', n.spde  = spde.a$n.spde)
mm <- model.matrix(~ DEPTH.std + Ttop50.std, X)[, -1] # using model matrix as factor variables are going to be included

### NO spatial field
stk.z <- inla.stack(data=list(MAC_PrAb=X$MAC_PrAb, link=1),
                    A=list(A.1, 1),
                    effects=list(ind.1, data.frame(z.intercept=1, mm)),
                    tag="Fit")

formula.z0 = as.formula(paste( "MAC_PrAb ~ 0 + z.intercept + ",  paste(colnames(X)[4:5], collapse = " + ")))

out.z0 <- inla(formula.z0, family="binomial", data=inla.stack.data(stk.z),
               control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.z), compute=TRUE, link=inla.stack.data(stk.z)$link),
               control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE))
summary(out.z0)

On Fri, 2017-08-18 at 02:10 -0700, Nikos Nikolioudakis wrote:
> I am running a binomial model and I get a huge sd on the intercept

> when a spatial random field is introduced in the model. I am

> struggling for quite some time with this and I cannot figure out
> whether this is a dataset related problem or not. For the moment I am
> using a coarse mesh, but I intend to utilize a finer mesh with land

> barriers as these are fisheries data.

Hi

a huge sd for the intercept where there also a spde in the model,
is usually because the spde have long range [almost intrinsic for the area you
look at], so that you nearly get a confounding in the mean.

you can force the spde to sum to zero adding constr=T, which will force a
separation of the constant...

H

--
Håvard Rue

messages.body_plain:
Yes, as Håvard wrote, a possible reason is confounding between the Intercept and the spatial effect. Note that the constr=TRUE option should in this case be used in the inla.spde2.matern() call, and not in the f() formula specification,  and that it results in an integrate-to-zero constrain across the spatial domain for the spatial effect.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Multilevel spatial model
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks!

I'd like to continue with this example:

> form <- out ~ 1 + f(cid, model = "bym", graph = "nb.adj") + f(sid, model = "iid")

Now I want to improve that model by:

1. Changing it from "bym" to "bym2";
2. Using PC priors for both random effects.

Following Riebler et al. (2016), the "bym2" part of the model can be specified as:

> f(cid, model = "bym2", graph = "nb.adj", scale.model = TRUE,
    hyper = list(
      phi = list(
        prior = "pc",
        param = c(0.5, 2/3),
        initial = -3),
      prec = list(
        prior = "pc.prec",
        param = c(0.2/0/31, 0.01),
        initial = 5)))

Or simply:

> f(cid, model = "bym2", graph = "nb.adj", scale.model = TRUE)

Right? What about the "iid" part of the model? Does the following

> f(sid, model = "iid",
    hyper = list(
      prec = list(
        prior = "pc.prec",
        param = c(0.3/0.31, 0.01))))

make sense (p. 9-10 of Simpson et al., 2017)? Or should I calculate U based on the data at hand, as demonstrated in this example(http://www.maths.bath.ac.uk/~jjf23/inla/multilevel.html)?

Many thanks.

Best,
Shige

The line calling INLA is:
result <- inla(form,family="poisson",E=E,data=stdata,verbose=inlaverbose,quantiles=q,control.inla=list(strategy=strategy))

Maybe some of the settings are what is causing this issue and I can post the full code if need be.

messages.body_plain:
> With regard to Q2 (and the point about the poor comparison), my Honours project has been around trying to understand all the theory behind this in order to re-make the comparisons and potentially test other similar problems. I would really appreciate any insight as to why this was a poor comparison and what would be a more appropriate way to compare the two methods? (I am guessing at why but if there is one thing learning all this has taught me is that I am painfully ignorant on too much!)

Comparing two methods is actually pretty hard. The one thing that's always true is you have to make sure the only point of difference is the thing you are comparing.

An example of that is here, where I compared the results for the same model fit in Stan and INLA.
https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/knitr/car-iar-poisson/stan_INLA_bym2.html

To make the model the same required some contortion (it was hard to make the priors match, for example).  If you want to run it yourself, it was done in RMarkdown, so just go up a level in github and download the corresponding file.

Now that was an easy case.  It's much harder to make a comparison with lgcp because we don't really fit the exact same models they do.  I think the closest we can do is the matern2d latent field (see inla.doc("matern2d")), which is Matern for nu = 1,2,3.

For the model, it's assumed that the GRF is zero outside the observation window, so you'll probably need to deal with the fact that that will be a difference. I don't know to what extent lgcp lets you play with boundary conditions.  When in doubt, extend the lattice far beyond the observation window, but make sure you do that for both methods (the idea is a level playing field).

It's really important that you don't plug parameter estimates from one model into the other one.  Because the models are subtly different, the "best" parameter values for each model will not be the same.  So if you estimate parameters on the lgcp model and plug them into INLA then you're putting INLA at a disadvantage.  Similarly, if you plug the "true" values that you simulated from into either method, you'll do badly.

Finally, you should meet the software on it's own home ground. For example, INLA is designed to do full approximate Bayesian inference, so it's not great to only test it with plug in parameter values.  Better practice would be to either do full inference or use int.stragegy="eb" for the internal emprical bayes procedure.

messages.subject: How to create linear combination of nested random components?
messages.subject_clean: How to create linear combination of nested random components?
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

My two-level disease mapping model has random effects at both the county-level and state-level (there are 3108 counties nested within 49 states):

> f <- out ~ 1 + f(county_id, model = "bym", graph = "nb.adj") + f(state_id, model = "iid")

I can easily create a linear combination of one random component and the intercept by:

> lcs1 <- inla.make.lincombs(county_id = diag(3108), "(Intercept)" = rep(1,3108))
> lcs2 <- inla.make.lincombs(state_id = diag(49), "(Intercept)" = rep(1,49))

But how can I create a linear combination of the two random components? I tried:

> lcs3 <- inla.make.lincombs(county_id = diag(3108), state_id = diag(49))

But it apparently did not work.

Many thanks.

Best,
Shige

messages.subject: Example for handling a Non-Stationary field
messages.subject_clean: Example for handling a Non-Stationary field
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
         I am using R-INLA to infer distributional parameters, given high dimensional spatial data. I then use the inferred distribution to generate more samples of the underlying field. I am new to R-INLA and spatial statistics in general, so please excuse any gross errors/missteps.

I did a trial run with a subset of the data, assuming stationarity. Everything checked out in that case, and I now want to move to the non-stationary case.

I have been following the reference 'Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA' so far, specifically sections 2.1 - 2.6. However, I have not been able to locate an equivalent example for the non-stationary case. I would be grateful if someone could point me to some examples that handle non-stationarity.

Regards.

I am trying to replicate the btopic107 in the Barrier Models examples, but inla crashes when trying to run the barrier-no-cov model. Models 'stationary-no-cov' and 'stationary-all-cov' run smoothly but then I get the following error.

        *** ERROR ***: The R-interface was not enabled at compile time: please recompile.

sh: line 1: 87007 Aborted                 (core dumped) '/usr/local/lib/R/site-library/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/inla.static' -b -s -v -t 30 '/tmp/RtmpBEjbHs/file214c1488df63/Model.ini' > /tmp/RtmpBEjbHs/file214c1488df63/Logfile.txt
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
In addition: Warning message:
In inla.model.properties.generic(inla.trim.family(model), (mm[names(mm) ==  :
  Model 'rgeneric' in section 'latent' is marked as 'experimental'; changes may appear at any time.
  Use this model with extra care!!! Further warnings are disabled.

Attached is the verbose = TRUE log in case is helps. I am running the models in R on a server (32 cores, 1TB ram, CentOS 7 (64 bit)).

Thank you
Nikos

messages.subject: Geometrical interpretation of hyperparametres of Matérn-model
messages.subject_clean: Geometrical interpretation of hyperparametres of Matérn-model
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I am pretty new to INLA and not a statistician, so I apologize if the question is too naive or not properly formulated!
I am predicting the probability of presence of forest. My data are in a 10x10 m raster resampled to 1x1 km units. The response (number of forest pixels to number of open land pixels in a 1km2 unit) is following a binomial distribution, and the predictors are various environmental variables (temperature, precipitation, terrain indices) - median value for 1km2 unit.

I am reproducing the approach of Beguin et al. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2012.00211.x/full) for hierarchical spatial modelling with spatially autocorrelated distributional data using a Matérn-model to account for spatial autocorrelation among units. (Their code is in the Supporting Information section.)

What I would like to know is how to geometrically interpret the hyperparametres of Matérn model - the precision (shape/scale) and range. If I got it right, the range refers to the range of spatial autocorrelation. Beguin et al. however use a logarithm of the range of spatial autocorrelation. Why should be a log(distance) used rather than just distance? And how can the precision (shape/scale) be interpreted?

Simplified example of the formula:
formula_matern <- n_success ~ temperature + precipitation + terrain +
                      f(node,
                        model='matern2d',
                        nrow=nrows,
                        ncol=ncols,
                        nu=1,
                        hyper=list(range=list(initial=log(range.sp.aut), fixed=TRUE), # ???
                                        prec=list(initial=precision, # ???
                                                      param=c(shape,scale)))) # ???

Thanks a lot for help!
Zofie
